Early voting passed 20 million ballots, with Democrats leading where party data exists (NPR, AP via The Hill). stories.title: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as reports point to Iran strikes after the midterms
stories.summary: The State Department ordered some embassy staff out of Saudi Arabia while U.S. and Israeli planners reportedly prepare new Iran strikes after Nov. 3.
story: The State Department ordered non-emergency staff and families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian targets, and CNBC reported the move alongside word that the U.S. is readying new Iran strikes after the Nov. 3 midterms. CNBC, citing The New York Times, said U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for renewed strikes. The likely targets are Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Trump has not approved them, per the same report.

CNBC's Oct. 24 report says U.S. embassies are tightening security as Iran threat warnings grow. A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio says Iranian plots against Americans have reached advanced stages (NBC News). The State Department also ordered further staff cuts at several posts, including in Lebanon, the UAE, Qatar and Jordan (CNBC). The war began on Feb. 28.

Iran has set its own terms. Its president demanded that the U.S. lift sanctions and end threats before talks can begin (Fox News). Iran's ambassador to Islamabad said Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, but Iranian state media later denied that report (AP via CNBC). A White House spokesperson said the blockade stays in full force. U.S. Central Command says most Iranian attacks on shipping fail and the strait remains open.
Fox News also reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for the U.S. and Israel to overthrow Iran as Brent crude hit a five-month high.
stories.flag: The strike plans come from anonymous officials cited by The New York Times. Neither the White House nor the Pentagon has confirmed them.
facts: The State Department ordered non-emergency embassy staff and families out of Saudi Arabia (CNBC, CNN).
The New York Times reported U.S. and Israeli plans for renewed strikes after Nov. 3 (CNBC).
Trump has not approved the strike plans, per the same report.
A U.S. intelligence memo says Iranian plots against Americans are in advanced stages (NBC News).
The U.S. naval blockade of Iran remains in place, a White House spokesperson said.
stories.left: Democrats and war-powers advocates argue that planning a major escalation for the day after an election shows politics is shaping war policy, and that Congress has not voted on a conflict now eight months old. They point to the evacuation orders as proof the administration expects Iranian retaliation against Americans abroad. They also note the oil spike is already raising prices at home, and want a diplomatic off-ramp pursued with the same energy as the strike planning.
stories.right: Supporters say a credible threat of force is what moves Tehran, and that delaying strikes until after Nov. 3 simply avoids handing Iran a propaganda win. Hawks say Iran's refusal to give up enriched uranium and its attacks on shipping leave little room for concessions, and that the blockade is the right pressure. A harder-line view, voiced in coverage like Fox's report on Netanyahu, holds that only regime change ends the threat. Others on the right worry about another open-ended war.
stories.next: Watch for any approval of strike plans after Nov. 3, and for oil prices as the Nov. 3 election nears.

stories.title: Justice Department sues to block Alaska Senate certification if the incumbent loses
stories.summary: Trump says he ordered the suit over a second candidate named Dan Sullivan; Democrats and some Republicans call it baseless.
story: The Justice Department filed suit on Thursday in federal court in Alaska to block the state from certifying its U.S. Senate result if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola (The Hill, CNN, Washington Examiner). The department argues that a second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, could confuse voters and tilt the race. President Trump said Friday, "I'm the one that said, do it," and called the second candidate a "fake" (The Hill, SF Chronicle).

The Alaska Supreme Court earlier ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan must be on the November ballot (Washington Examiner). Attorney General Todd Blanche said the suit "does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska's election" (The Hill). Common Cause, represented by the ACLU, has moved to intervene against the department (The Hill). Sabato's Crystal Ball moved the race to Leans Democratic (Washington Examiner).

Reaction crossed party lines. Peltola called the suit a "desperate attempt" to cling to power (The Hill). Sen. Lisa Murkowski said "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit" (CNN). Election law professor Derek Muller called the theory "strange and unusual" and noted Alaska's ranked-choice voting lets voters rank both Sullivans (CNN). Sullivan's campaign said it will "let the DOJ complaint run its course". Ranked-choice tabulation is expected to begin Nov. 18.
Gov. Gavin Newsom said it should "scare the hell out of everybody" (SF Chronicle).
facts: The suit was filed Thursday, Oct. 22, in U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska.
Trump said he directed the Justice Department to file it.
The Alaska Supreme Court had already put Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot.
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, said the department should not have filed the suit (CNN).
Ranked-choice tabulation is expected to start Nov. 18 (CNN).
stories.left: Democrats say the suit tries to pre-build a path to overturning an election the incumbent might lose, and that voters can tell two candidates apart, especially with party labels and ranked-choice voting. They see it as part of a pattern, pairing it with the California ballot fight, and they note even Republican Murkowski objects. They want the courts to dismiss it quickly so no one questions the result.
stories.right: Supporters say a same-name candidate recruited to siphon votes is a real distortion, and that the department is entitled to ask a court to protect voters from confusion before the result is final. Conservative commentators call the ballot situation corrupt (Washington Examiner), and say the suit seeks a remedy only if the result is affected. Even sympathetic Republicans, however, have been cool on the legal theory.
stories.blindspot: Right-leaning outlets mostly relayed the department's case; few defended the legal theory in depth.
stories.next: Watch for a ruling on Common Cause's motion to intervene, and for how a court treats the suit before Nov. 3.

stories.title: Early voting runs far ahead of 2022 as Democrats lead where party data exists
stories.summary: Totals differ by tracker, but turnout is up sharply in Texas, Kansas and North Carolina with nine days to go.
story: NPR reported Friday that more than 19 million people have already voted. Other trackers put the total higher, with NBC News showing roughly 27 million mail and early in-person votes, and the Associated Press counting over 20 million across 46 states (NBC News, The Hill). Different dates and data sources explain much of the gap. Texas led with 2.36 million ballots and California followed with 2.32 million.

A New York Times analysis found early voting up about 74% in Texas, 69% in Kansas and 41% in Maine compared with 2022, while Iowa is down about 6% (via Axios and The Hill). North Carolina turnout is up 37%, with Democrats casting twice as many ballots as Republicans (Axios). Michigan and Georgia are high but similar to four years ago.

In states with party registration data, Democrats are voting at higher rates than Republicans. Analysts caution that early voters tend to be more engaged than average, so the numbers are a weak predictor. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, and Democrats need a net gain of four seats (Fox News). A Fox News poll has the Texas Senate race tied at 49% between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. House Speaker Mike Johnson said he is "very bullish" (Fox News).
facts: Over 20 million early ballots were counted by the AP across 46 states.
Texas early voting is up 74% from 2022 (NYT via The Hill).
North Carolina turnout is up 37% (Axios).
Republicans hold the Senate 53-47; Democrats need a net four seats.
A Fox News poll shows the Texas Senate race tied at 49% each.
stories.left: Democrats see enthusiasm in the surge, especially in North Carolina and Texas, and in polls showing them ahead in competitive Senate races. They argue the numbers undercut Republican claims of a quiet base, and want to push turnout further in the final days with Obama's planned travel to Michigan, Ohio and Georgia.
stories.right: Republicans say early ballots are banked by engaged voters who would have voted anyway, and that Election Day turnout and independents decide the outcome. Speaker Johnson says he is bullish, and Republicans point to a tied Texas race and to ad spending in Kansas, Texas and Nebraska as signs the map is not as bad as Democrats claim.
stories.next: Watch Georgia early voting through Oct. 30 and the final week of rallies before Election Day on Nov. 3.

stories.title: DOJ gives California counties 48 hours to quarantine ballots of suspected noncitizens
stories.summary: Letters went to at least 18 counties as a hearing on the department's request to set aside 20,000 ballots nears.
story: The Justice Department sent letters Friday, Oct. 23, to county registrars across California, giving them 48 hours to act on lists of voters it suspects are noncitizens (SF Chronicle). At least 18 counties got letters, per the LA County registrar's office. Contra Costa's list had 407 names, Merced's 177 and San Bernardino's 1,133. The letters ask counties to sequester, not cancel, mail ballots where citizenship cannot be verified (SF Chronicle, KQED).

Last week the department sued to block the state from counting about 20,000 ballots, and a hearing before Judge David Carter is set for Tuesday (Fox News). The Ninth Circuit ordered California to respond to an emergency DOJ request by noon Saturday (Fox News). U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli says investigators determined all 20,000 people are noncitizens. A county review of a 200-record sample found 112 corresponded to canceled or inactive registrations.

Secretary of State Shirley Weber rejected the demands, saying her office would not disenfranchise voters based on "unverifiable information or methodology". LA County Registrar Dean Logan called the letters a "posture of intimidation" (SF Chronicle). LA County alone has processed 331,000 ballots, and officials say separating ballots already processed is impossible. Federal officials first alleged 190,000 noncitizens are registered; the state disputes that.
stories.flag: The DOJ says the 20,000 list is verified noncitizens. State and county officials dispute the list's accuracy. No court has ruled on it.
facts: Letters went to at least 18 California counties on Oct. 23 (SF Chronicle).
Federal authorities charged 28 lawful permanent residents earlier this week (Fox News).
A county review found 112 of 200 sampled records were canceled or inactive.
A hearing before Judge David Carter is set for Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Weber says the state will not act on the lists.
stories.left: Critics say a 48-hour demand nine days before an election, built on a list officials say contains canceled registrations, is intimidation that could delay certification and disenfranchise eligible voters. They note citizens have been wrongly flagged in past purges and that counties lack access to federal citizenship records.
stories.right: Supporters say noncitizen voting is illegal and that California officials refuse to check obvious problems. They point to Essayli's claim that all 20,000 are noncitizens and to the 28 federal charges as evidence the problem is real. They say sequestering, rather than canceling, ballots protects both the voter and the count while eligibility is checked.
stories.next: Watch the Tuesday, Oct. 27 hearing before Judge Carter and any Ninth Circuit ruling before it.

stories.title: Bay Area's regional transit tax faces a split electorate nine days out
stories.summary: The 14-year sales tax would raise about $980 million a year; agencies warn of deep service cuts if it fails.
story: The Regional Transit Measure is on the Nov. 3 ballot in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara and San Francisco counties (KQED voter guide). It adds a sales tax for 14 years: 0.5% in four counties and 1% in San Francisco. The ballot language estimates about $980 million a year (League of Women Voters). Money would go to BART, Muni, Caltrain and AC Transit.

Agencies say that without it, Muni could cut service 30% and cancel about 20 lines, BART could close 15 stations, and Caltrain would close more than a third of its stations (KQED, SF Chronicle). A report says Bay Bridge delays would double if transit measures fail (KQED). An Embold Research poll found 48% in favor, 34% opposed and 18% undecided. The SF Chronicle endorsed it.

The opposition committee, backed by the Contra Costa Taxpayers Association with former state Sen. Steve Glazer, calls the tax regressive and says agencies should use existing money first. Spokesperson Marc Joffe said, "We don't agree that the failure of RTM would necessitate slashing service." The pro-measure campaign calls those arguments "not grounded in reality" (KQED).
stories.blindspot: Coverage found is from left-leaning and center outlets; the opposition's view appears mostly through those outlets' reporting.
facts: The tax runs 14 years: 0.5% in four counties, 1% in San Francisco.
It would raise about $980 million a year (ballot language).
BART says it could close 15 stations without it.
An Embold poll found 48% yes, 34% no, 18% undecided.
The measure needs voter approval on Nov. 3.
stories.left: Supporters argue transit is basic infrastructure, that a service death spiral hurts low-income riders and the climate, and that a regional measure is the only workable fix. Some progressives prefer a business tax over a sales tax but still back the measure as the available lifeline.
stories.right: Opponents argue the tax is regressive, that agencies should cut costs and reallocate capital money before asking for more, and that the cut threats are scare tactics. They want accountability on spending before a new 14-year tax.
stories.next: Watch for new polling and the Nov. 3 vote.

stories.title: Fed meets Oct. 27-28 with a hold expected and a December hike in play
stories.summary: Inflation at 3.7% and oil near $103 keep rate-hike bets alive, though traders see no move this week.
story: The Federal Open Market Committee meets Oct. 27-28, with the decision due Wednesday at 2 p.m. ET. Traders see a 92% chance of no change and a 78% chance of a December hike (CNBC). The Fed raised its range to 3.75%-4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023 (Fox Business). September CPI rose 3.7% from a year earlier (CNBC).

Chair Kevin Warsh declined to preview the decision, saying he does not prejudge meetings (CNBC, Axios). Vice Chair Jefferson, New York Fed President John Williams and Governor Waller have signaled the Fed could wait in October (CNBC). Goldman Sachs expects a second hike in December (CNBC). CNBC's analysis warned Warsh could still surprise since he rejects forward guidance.

Oil is the pressure point. WTI settled at $103.27 on Friday, up 3.82%, per live market data, and CNBC reported Brent topped $116. Critics on the right argue rate hikes cannot fix a supply shock caused by the Hormuz blockade (Washington Examiner). Others say the hike was needed to hold inflation expectations (Fox Business).
facts: The decision is Wednesday, Oct. 28 at 2 p.m. ET.
The Fed range is 3.75%-4.00%.
September CPI was 3.7% year over year.
WTI crude is $103.27, up 3.82% Friday.
Traders see a 78% chance of a December hike (CNBC).
stories.left: Progressives and many economists warn that hiking into an oil shock risks job losses and slower growth without lowering energy prices, and that the war the administration started is driving the inflation. They want the Fed to weigh employment and a weak September jobs report.
stories.right: Some conservatives argue the Fed is punishing households for a supply shock it cannot fix by drilling, while others say inflation near 3.7% demands action and that Warsh is right to stay independent. The common thread is blame for the Hormuz blockade and war spending.
stories.next: Watch the Wednesday, Oct. 28 decision and Warsh's press conference.

stories.title: Stocks face Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon earnings after a week of AI-funding fears
stories.summary: About 160 S&P 500 companies report as the AI buildout's debt load worries investors.
story: The S&P 500 fell 0.52% on Friday to 7,623.68, the Dow lost 1.23% to 52,215.16 and the Nasdaq slid 0.21% to 25,955.34 (live market data). About 160 S&P 500 companies report this week (CNBC). Alphabet and Microsoft report Wednesday after the close, and Amazon Thursday. Boeing and Eli Lilly also report.

Analysts expect Alphabet revenue up about 25%, Microsoft earnings up 14.3%, and roughly flat earnings per share but double-digit revenue growth for Amazon (CNBC, LSEG data). Evercore's Mark Mahaney said hyperscalers could disclose capital spending higher by as much as $100 billion. Alphabet fell last quarter after raising its capex forecast (CNBC). GOOGL closed Friday at $320.21, down 1.24%.

The backdrop is AI financing worry. Neocloud stocks CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are each down over 30% in October, and CoreWeave's credit default swap spreads passed 11% (CNBC). SK Hynix scrapped a $10 billion Solidigm IPO (Bloomberg). Higher oil and bond yields add pressure, with the 10-year Treasury at 4.99%.
stories.why: Earnings from the three largest AI spenders will show whether investors still reward capex. Weak guidance or higher spending could extend the AI selloff, while a Fed hold would remove one risk.
facts: Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28 after the close; Amazon reports Oct. 29 (live data).
The Dow fell 1.23% Friday to 52,215.16.
The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.99%.
CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are each down over 30% in October (CNBC).
Apple reports Nov. 2 and Nvidia Nov. 18.
stories.next: Watch Oct. 28 after the close for Alphabet and Microsoft, then Amazon on Oct. 29.

stories.title: IBM's Anderon builds a 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry backed by a $1 billion federal award
stories.summary: The Albany, New York foundry aims to let quantum hardware firms get chips made without building their own fab.
story: IEEE Spectrum reports the Commerce Department finalized a CHIPS and Science Act R&D award of up to $1 billion for Anderon, a quantum foundry IBM created this year. IBM is matching with $1 billion in cash, intellectual property and staff. The government takes a minority, non-controlling stake (CNBC, May).

Anderon is based in Albany, New York, and will run a 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry building on IBM's Albany NanoTech work, where IBM has made quantum wafers for more than five years, per CEO Mukesh Khare (IEEE Spectrum). The idea mirrors TSMC for conventional chips: customers design, the foundry builds.

Commerce also finalized up to $375 million for GlobalFoundries and up to $100 million each for Rigetti, D-Wave, Quantinuum and PsiQuantum (IEEE Spectrum). Rigetti is reportedly in talks with Anderon. IBM's CEO has said quantum will have a measurable earnings impact by 2028 or 2029 (CNBC).
stories.flag: The finalization date differs across sources (September per TipRanks headline cited in search); check Commerce or IBM releases.
stories.why: Shared quantum fabrication could cut the cost of entry for hardware startups and standardize wafer processes, as shared foundries did for conventional chips.
facts: The award is up to $1 billion from Commerce under the CHIPS Act.
IBM contributes a matching $1 billion.
Anderon runs a 300 mm wafer foundry in Albany, New York.
GlobalFoundries gets up to $375 million.
The government takes minority, non-controlling stakes.
stories.next: Watch for outside customers signing with Anderon, including Rigetti.

stories.title: NASA-led model says Thwaites Glacier could add more to sea level rise than earlier estimates
stories.summary: A Nature Communications study treats the grounding zone as a wide band, roughly doubling some projections by 2100.
story: A NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory model, built with UC Irvine and Dartmouth and published Oct. 12 in Nature Communications, treats Thwaites Glacier's grounding zone as a wide band rather than a sharp line (JPL). In some simulations the glacier's contribution to sea level rise reached roughly double current projections by century's end.

The authors say the approach reduces uncertainty about the glacier's long-term impact. Earlier NASA work pointed the other way on pace: a 2017 study found models overstated ocean melt and cut projected 50-year ice loss by about 7% (NASA). A 2019 study found a cavity under the glacier about two-thirds the area of Manhattan (NASA).
Scientists estimate a full collapse would raise global sea level by several feet, and ice flow has doubled over about three decades (NASA Science).
stories.flag: Results come from model simulations, and different models and ocean scenarios give different answers.
stories.why: Coastal planners, including those around San Francisco Bay, depend on glacier projections. A wider uncertainty band on a major ice source raises the high-end sea level scenarios.
facts: The study appeared Oct. 12 in Nature Communications.
JPL led it with UC Irvine and Dartmouth.
Some simulations roughly doubled current projections by 2100.
A full Thwaites collapse would raise seas by several feet.
A 2017 NASA study had lowered projected loss by about 7%.
stories.next: Watch for independent modeling groups testing the grounding-zone approach.

stories.title: Prior prescribed burns cut giant sequoia deaths in California's 2020-21 megafires
stories.summary: A study of 26,403 trees found prescribed fire within a decade lowered mortality odds by 77%.
story: A Nature Communications study by Dixon, Das and Jin analyzed 26,403 giant sequoias across 19 groves in Sequoia and Kings Canyon national parks, using lidar, stem maps and satellite imagery (Nature Communications). It estimated mortality after the Castle Fire in 2020 and the KNP Complex fire in 2021.

Overall mortality was 30.2%. Prescribed burns within the prior 10 years cut mortality odds by 77%, so treated trees were roughly four times as likely to survive. Counterfactual modeling suggested the burns prevented at least 1,888 deaths, and treating every grove would have saved about 3,888 more trees.
NASA, which funded the work, noted that 19% of mature giant sequoias range-wide were destroyed in those two years (NASA Science).
stories.why: It gives managers numbers for prescribed fire, a tool California is expanding to lower megafire risk.
facts: The study covered 26,403 trees in 19 groves.
Mortality overall was 30.2%.
Prior burns cut mortality odds by 77%.
At least 1,888 deaths were prevented, per modeling.
19% of mature sequoias were destroyed in 2020-21.
stories.next: Watch how park managers and the Forest Service scale up burns before the next fire season.

stories.title: AI infrastructure stocks slide as neocloud debt and credit spreads widen
stories.summary: CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are each down over 30% in October as lenders price in more risk.
story: CNBC reported that shares of neocloud providers CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN fell sharply this week and are each down well over 30% for October. CoreWeave's credit default swap spreads widened past 11%, a level generally viewed as distress, and its 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes yield above 15%.

Meta, Oracle and Nvidia faced the largest-ever spreads on credit default swaps tied to their bonds (CNBC). CoreWeave's total debt is above $51 billion. HSBC's analyst said debt market woes and moderating large language model revenues are worsening structural concerns, and Gartner predicted 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030.

Elsewhere, Korea's Elice fell 32% in its debut and Australia's NextDC dropped 39.5% after cutting guidance (CNBC). SK Hynix scrapped a $10 billion Solidigm IPO; Bloomberg cited regulator and shareholder concerns, while the company's filing cited capital market conditions.
stories.why: The AI buildout is increasingly debt-funded. If credit tightens for neoclouds, Nvidia and the labs that rent their capacity may feel it.
facts: Neocloud stocks are each down over 30% in October (CNBC).
CoreWeave debt exceeds $51 billion.
Solidigm's $10 billion IPO was pulled.
Gartner says 80% of neoclouds may cease independent operations by 2030.
Earnings from hyperscalers this week will update capex.
stories.next: Watch Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon capex commentary on Oct. 28-29.

stories.title: Nvidia releases open Nemotron 3.5 models for enterprise agents and local PCs
stories.summary: A 120-billion-parameter Super VL targets companies; Bolt models run locally on RTX Spark PCs.
story: TechCrunch reported Nvidia launched open-weight models on Oct. 19. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120-billion-parameter model for enterprise agents. Nvidia says it matches Nemotron 3 Ultra on instruction following and tool-use accuracy with fewer parameters.

Two Bolt models run locally: Bolt 74B-A9B at 74 billion parameters for local agentic tasks, and a smaller Bolt E4B for conversational agents. They target PCs with Nvidia's RTX Spark chip and DGX Spark workstations. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now; Bolt E4B is due later this month.

Nvidia claims Super VL completes post-trained tasks, such as document intelligence and insurance claims, faster than competing Anthropic and OpenAI models. Named users include EY, Ramp, CrowdStrike, Perplexity and Salesforce. These are vendor claims, not independent benchmarks.
stories.flag: Performance comparisons are Nvidia's own claims.
stories.why: Open models that run locally cut cost and data-privacy risk for agents, and push Nvidia further from chips into the model layer.
facts: Super VL has 120 billion parameters.
Bolt 74B-A9B and Super VL are available now.
Bolt E4B is due later in October.
Nvidia named EY, Ramp and CrowdStrike as adopters.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 18.
stories.next: Watch for independent benchmarks of Super VL against Anthropic and OpenAI models.

briefs: Agility Robotics says its Digit humanoid has logged more than 65,000 operational hours, and Toyota will use seven in a Canadian plant under a robots-as-a-service deal (TechCrunch, IEEE Spectrum).
California billionaire-tax Prop 40 leads narrowly in polls, but Props 41 and 42 could nullify it, and PPIC and IGS polls differ (CalMatters).
Newsom is weighing commuting some or all of California's 563 remaining death sentences before leaving office (KQED).
BART reports crimes against riders per million trips fell 67% between December 2024 and June 2026 (KQED).
Newsom endorsed Prop 42, the wealth-tax ban, and opposes Prop 39, the voter ID measure (CalMatters).
